Chapter 7: Accountability and the Burden of Responsibility
As the war drags on, there’s this growing shadow—accountability. It hangs over everything, pushing the people who made the big decisions to finally face what’s happened because of them. Some folks try to justify the choices they made, pointing to the facts they had at the time. Others admit they got things wrong, but insist their hearts were in the right place. And across the country, everyone’s caught up in searching for someone to blame.
Picture a former advisor in the White House, sitting alone in his office. He’s holding a letter from a soldier’s mother. She’s asking a simple question—why did her son have to die? The words themselves are straightforward, but the pain behind them? It’s enormous. He finds himself replaying those old meetings, the heated debates, the moments he could have spoken up but chose not to. The weight of responsibility feels crushing. And honestly, there are no easy answers.
Meanwhile, Congress is holding hearings to investigate how the war was handled. Witnesses step forward, talking about missed chances, bad intelligence, and the pressure everyone felt to just go along. Some speak with frustration—others, with deep regret. People all over the country are tuning in, hoping for a little honesty and a sense that someone will finally be held accountable. For many, it’s the first real glimpse into how decisions actually get made—the compromises, the doubts, and the very human mistakes.
But here’s something important to remember: accountability isn’t only about pointing fingers or pinning blame. It’s about seeing how even good intentions can spiral into bad results, and how even the smartest people can make costly errors. It’s about learning from what’s happened, so we don’t stumble into the same traps again. Sure, the process is painful—there’s no way around that. But it’s also the only way forward. Without it, there’s no healing, no real progress, and no hope for a better future.
